rolesData.context: Founder / Consultant — Retail Development, Sourcing & Business Systems
rolesData.about: More Margin Co. helps retailers and suppliers develop sales channels, plan assortments, open stores, and build practical reporting tools. Engagements draw on Nicolas Goureau’s operating experience and longstanding sourcing and retail relationships, from commercial planning through implementation.

chapters.text:
I established More Margin Co. as a way to put longstanding relationships and operating experience to work on specific business needs. Suppliers come to me to explore new retail channels; retailers need help with assortments, stores, and the systems behind them. My contribution is connecting the commercial question with what it takes to deliver.

The DJI Fifth Avenue flagship was an eight-month engagement spanning 2025–2026, beginning after site selection. We built financial models to assess the store both on its own and as part of STC’s existing business. The standalone case showed limited profitability, but the projected benefit to the wider business made a stronger case for proceeding.
chapters.cap: DJI Fifth Avenue — the US flagship, built to a new store standard.

chapters.text:
Once the DJI project cleared that gate, I worked through the lease and build process with the team. Using specifications from DJI’s China headquarters, I developed the layout, merchandising plan, training processes, and replenishment models covering supply from China and the New Jersey warehouse. We obtained contractor bids, carried out the build, and integrated the operation with STC’s customer, warehouse, product-information, and accounting systems.

NuvoMed presented a different opportunity. I had worked with its parent company for more than eight years on sourcing and importing products. With national retail distribution already established, they asked me to help find additional markets. We identified outdoor retail, drawing on my experience and relationships in that sector. I later helped develop a drive-aisle PDQ display program to support their expansion at Home Depot and Lowe’s.

Alongside these engagements, I help retailers decide what to carry, how to price it, and what to stop buying.
chapters.cap: NuvoMed — into the active sports retail market.

chapters.text:
The DJI store opened around February–March 2026 after receiving its New York City certificate of occupancy and approval from China headquarters, with the operating processes and systems connections in place. I remain a contact for STC when similar complex projects arise.

For NuvoMed, our work brought products into Fun Town RV, Camping World, REI, and other retailers. The home-improvement display program created another route to expand the offer. I estimate that the combined work contributed more than $5 million in revenue over ten months. The relationship continues, with the company returning to me as new needs arise.
chapters.cap: Assortment planning across a roster of clients.

chapters.text:
A store opening or a new retail placement also needs useful information behind it. I have built dashboards for small businesses and e-commerce operations, bringing scattered data into a form stakeholders can access and understand.

I approach the analysis with confirmation bias in mind: a dashboard should help people examine what is happening, including results that challenge their expectations. Across these engagements, the aim is to leave people with an operation, a sales channel, or a practical tool they can use.

Alongside client engagements, I continually develop my own tools to address recurring business needs and make them available as part of future client work. These are ongoing product-development projects, separate from client deployments.
chapters.cap: Dashboards built so operators can act on their own numbers.

rolesData.role: Director of Sourcing, Retail, Aftermarket & E-Commerce
rolesData.context: Retail Development, Private Label & Connected Operations
rolesData.clientsIntro: Four closer looks at the spaces, products and processes behind the work.

clients.name: Planning the new stores
clients.did: I used longstanding vendor relationships to develop a larger retail offer alongside the RV business. My work covered the layout, fixture planning, product placement, branding and graphics, followed by planograms and merchandising guides. The aim was to translate the concept into an arrangement that store teams could set up, maintain and replenish.

clients.name: Corsicana flagship
clients.kind: Opened March 2022 · Retail and RV sales
clients.did: Corsicana opened in March 2022, following my arrival the previous November. Within the 65,000-square-foot facility, approximately 10,000 square feet was dedicated to retail, alongside a full-service café and restaurant, service counter and six checkout lanes. I designed the branding, layout and graphics for both retail and RV sales, including the sales tower and training rooms.

clients.name: Factory-direct products
clients.did: The KAMPTIME sewer-hose display shows one tangible part of the private-label program: a frequently purchased RV accessory sourced directly and presented under a house brand. My responsibilities connected supplier sourcing with the product offer, packaging, pricing and merchandising. The broader program concentrated on the top 50 selling products under KAMPTIME and USA Rec. Supply, our two house brands.

clients.name: Logistics and internal ordering
clients.did: I moved products into third-party logistics and developed an internal ordering portal for dealerships and head office, with automatic replenishment supporting stock availability. Store inventory also supported orders from the company website and marketplaces. The objective was to make ordering, fulfillment and the associated accounting easier to manage, with fewer errors and less overhead.

rolesData.about: Fun Town RV is a privately held RV dealership group selling recreational vehicles alongside parts, accessories, maintenance and related services. My work focused on developing its retail and aftermarket business, connecting store design and private-label products with purchasing, online sales and fulfillment.

chapters.text:
I joined Fun Town RV in November 2021 to develop private-label products and redesign how its stores looked, worked and presented merchandise. The immediate assignment included the new Corsicana location, which opened in March 2022. It was an ambitious starting point: a 65,000-square-foot facility with approximately 10,000 square feet of retail space, a full-service café and restaurant, a service counter and six checkout lanes.

The store brief exposed a wider operating challenge. Locations maintained separate parts catalogs and identifiers, making consolidated reporting and ordering difficult. Retail transactions ran through a system primarily designed for RV dealership operations, products were purchased through distributors, and there was little effective online visibility for the assortment. Improving the stores meant addressing the information, purchasing and fulfillment behind them.

I reported directly to COO Jeff England. Many of the approaches I proposed were new to the company, so explaining how they worked—and why they were worth adopting—was an important part of securing approval. We brought different experiences and processes to the work. Building trust and finding a workable approach together came before greater independence.
chapters.cap: Planning a 65,000 sq ft store and the systems to support it.

chapters.text:
I began connecting the assortment through a shared product database, organizing more than 30,000 SKUs to support more consistent product information, ordering and reporting. Using Shopify and its plugin ecosystem, I developed the retail platform around POS, mobile checkout, the website and marketplace sales. We introduced it at one location before expanding to six across two divisions of the business.

Alongside the systems work, I selected the top 50 selling products as candidates for factory-direct sourcing. I drew on my supplier relationships to develop an assortment under two house brands—KAMPTIME and USA Rec. Supply—connecting product selection, packaging, pricing and store presentation. This gave the dealerships an alternative to buying those products solely through distributors.

The physical stores needed the same consistency. I designed branding, layouts and graphics, developed planograms and merchandising standards, and issued merchandising guides to help teams put the approach into practice. At Corsicana, my design responsibilities extended beyond retail into the RV sales environment, including the sales tower and training rooms.

I also developed the ordering and logistics operation around the products. Inventory moved into third-party logistics, while an internal web portal allowed both dealerships and head office to place store orders and support automatic replenishment. The work connected purchasing and stock availability with how products reached the sales floor and the customer.
chapters.cap: The first newly branded store — retail floor and fulfillment center in one.

chapters.text:
The internal sourcing business reached $3 million in sales in under a year, with Fun Town’s dealerships as its main customers. On the selected factory-direct products, the reported margin increased from 28% to 79%—a 51-percentage-point improvement. That result applied to those products, rather than the margin of the entire business.

The platform expanded from its first location to six across two business divisions. The website and marketplace channels created additional routes to customers, with store inventory also used to fulfill online orders. Product information, retail transactions and ordering were becoming parts of a shared operation rather than separate tasks at each location.

The logistics and internal ordering work reduced errors and overhead and made accounting easier. Just as importantly, the business had practical foundations it could use: its own product offer, a larger retail presence, clearer merchandise standards and new ways to sell and replenish stock.
chapters.cap: Private label: two house brands, 28% to 79% margin.

chapters.text:
This assignment reinforced that introducing a new way of working requires more than designing the solution. I had to explain unfamiliar capabilities, work through questions and approvals, and adapt my approach to the organization’s pace. I was there to build a business for Fun Town, and the operation needed to make sense to the people who would run it.

The work crossed sourcing, stores, data, sales and logistics. Each part depended on the others, and adoption required clear processes, useful guidance and people who understood their responsibilities. I carried a substantial share of the development myself; the experience strengthened my conviction that building the team and its ability to use the work is part of delivering the business.
chapters.cap: Logistics: 3PL plus an internal ordering and replenishment portal.

rolesData.context: Business development, sourcing and operations consulting, alongside the creation of the FitBox venture.
rolesData.about: Big Box Group provided sourcing, product development, sales, logistics and operational consulting to retail, e-commerce and consumer-product businesses. Its work connected established supplier relationships with opportunities to improve how products reached customers.

chapters.text:
I worked with suppliers and past business partners to find additional sales channels for their products and improve how those products reached stores and customers. I drew on international relationships built over more than twenty years, connecting sourcing and product decisions with sales, logistics and the practical requirements of the businesses involved.

FitBox was a separate venture I created during this period. After leaving Camping World, I continued working with real-estate contacts from the Camping World and Gander project, contributing an operator’s perspective on what could come next for large retail properties.

I kept seeing spaces that were the wrong size for many potential occupants. A smaller business might need 2,000 square feet, while a vacant store offered 35,000. Finding one tenant for the entire building could be difficult—and would leave the property dependent on that business. I saw an opportunity to rethink both the space and the operating model.
chapters.cap: Finding another use for empty big-box space.

chapters.text:
In the consulting work, I connected supplier capabilities with opportunities in other sales channels and examined how products moved into stores and onto shelves. The work brought together sourcing, product development, sales and logistics, with attention to the changes a client’s operation would need to make the commercial opportunity practical.

For FitBox, I developed a model in which we would master-lease a large vacant space and divide it into smaller premises for independent businesses. Fitness, recovery, food and everyday services could serve overlapping customers while retaining their own operations.

The tenant mix and the layout had to work together. Shared reception, lockers, showers and common areas would give smaller operators access to facilities they would otherwise have to build and maintain individually. The aim was to reduce duplicated costs and make the space more accessible to those businesses.

I worked through the relationship between the master rent, smaller tenant leases, common-area charges and the cost of managing shared facilities. The model needed to make commercial sense for the property, the venture and the participating businesses. I also raised capital for the first prototype, contingent on signing a lease.
chapters.cap: FitBox: smaller businesses sharing a larger space.

chapters.text:
The consulting work produced operational recommendations, including projected improvements for a client’s sales and logistics operation. Those projections were separate from FitBox and should not be presented as realized savings.

FitBox progressed from concept development to capital raised for a first prototype, with a lease signing planned for April 2020. When COVID changed the circumstances, we stopped before signing and returned the funds. No investor lost money.

The project did not reach an operating launch. Its proposed benefits—shared infrastructure, smaller commitments for individual businesses and less dependence on a single tenant—remained part of the business model rather than demonstrated operating results.
chapters.cap: Spreading the dependence across several tenants.

chapters.text:
My contribution began with an operator’s view of a real-estate problem: what would make this space usable, affordable and practical for the businesses inside it? Answering that meant connecting customer demand, supplier and operator relationships, space planning, shared costs and the economics of the overall venture.

That is the transferable part of this experience. I can identify an opportunity, develop the business model around it and work through what would be required to bring it into use. It also requires judgment about when to proceed. With FitBox, the circumstances changed before the lease commitment, and we stopped and returned the capital.
chapters.cap: Making the space work for the businesses inside it.

rolesData.context: Reporting directly to Marcus Lemonis, I led branding, store layouts, merchandising, and product development across acquired outdoor businesses and helped develop new RV retail formats.
rolesData.about: Camping World combines RV dealerships, service, parts, accessories, and outdoor retail. During my tenure, its expansion brought together businesses with different customers, assortments, and store formats, creating opportunities to connect product development with a broader national footprint.

plStory.t: Start with what the customer needs
plStory.d: Every brand began the same way: a category where we were selling somebody else's label at somebody else's margin. Nepallo came out of fishing and sun protection, aimed squarely at Columbia PFG and Huk. Outfitta came out of active apparel. Before a single sample existed there was a customer, a price tier, a competitor, and a reason to exist — then the identity, the color standards, the hangtag, and the fabric story that had to survive being held in a customer's hand.

An owned brand needs to give the customer a reason to choose it, through the product, the price, or both. Temp360 was the clearest case: rechargeable heated base layers, socks, and glove liners, built around a technology story a customer could understand in three seconds on a shelf. That meant specs written on our side, factory samples, testing, and packaging that sold the feature before the price.

plStory.t: Get it from the factory to the store
plStory.d: The work continued well beyond design. Each line was sourced factory-direct through a vendor network built over twenty years, negotiated, imported, cleared, labeled, warehoused, and allocated across a national fleet of stores. Landed cost was modeled before a single unit shipped, because the margin only exists if the freight math works.
plStory.brands: Grill World · Tow Center of America · camping hardlines

plStory.d: The portfolio kept widening. Marine brought Dockmate for docking hardware, lighting and ladders, Covermate for boat and pontoon covers, a pontoon furniture and hardware line, and Gladiator for towables and watersports. Fishing ran from value combos up to an angler tier of rods and reels. Hunting added value and best-tier fieldwear, Trophy Boss for deer gear, waterfowl and archery labels, and two tactical brands for the shooting customer. Flex came in from the other direction — a West Coast watch and watersports lifestyle brand. Each one needed its own identity, tiering, sourcing, and shelf logic.
plStory.brands: Dockmate · Covermate · Gladiator · Trophy Boss · Flex

plStory.t: Make it work in each sales channel
plStory.d: Each brand ran its own site, its own marketplace listings, wholesale accounts, and the retail floor — one assortment with different pricing rules and content needs in each channel. Margin on private label ran far above national brands, and the owned brands gave customers a range they could not buy elsewhere.
plStory.brands: Forge · Simple Nest · Dockmate · 50+ brands in total

plCats.d: Everyday camp and hike wear, performance active apparel, fishing and sun protection, loungewear, heated and cooled technical apparel, and value sun-and-water goods.
plCats.vs: L.L.Bean, Eddie Bauer, Under Armour, Columbia PFG

plCats.d: Tents, sleeping bags, chairs, cots, canopies, and camp accessories across an opening-price tier, a family good/better tier, and a specialty best tier.
Hard and soft-sided coolers, tumblers, and insulated drinkware, plus a full grilling and outdoor cooking line.
RV interior and home accessories for kitchen, living, bedroom and bath, towing and exterior products including hitches, chocks and levelling blocks, and an unbranded utility line.
Rods, reels, combos, bait, tackle and bags across value and angler tiers, plus docking, biminis, boat covers, pontoon, and watersports lines.
Value and best-tier fieldwear, hunting gear, waterfowl and deer-specific brands, archery, and two tactical shooting brands.

chapters.text:
I worked directly with Marcus Lemonis as Camping World expanded across Gander Outdoors, The House, Overton’s, and Specialty Outdoor Retail—a group of independent outdoor retailers with multiple locations. My responsibility was to turn the commercial direction into products, branding, layouts, and merchandising that teams could put into practice.

The Gander reopening program brought particular urgency. Stores ranged from approximately 20,000 to 100,000 square feet, and a consistent brand presentation still had to work within very different buildings. We needed to connect assortments, fixtures, suppliers, and store teams while making disciplined decisions about how much inventory each location could support.
chapters.cap: Connecting acquired businesses with store execution.

chapters.text:
I led the branding, layout, merchandising, and product work, coordinating with colleagues, vendors, and operating teams. I ran point on the initial store sets and developed changes as we discovered what worked on the floor. A plan could look complete on paper and still need substantial adjustment once fixtures, merchandise, and customers occupied the space.

The product program covered RV parts, hunting, fishing, shooting sports, active sports, cycling, apparel, skiing, and convenience, alongside service-related store concepts. I developed private-label identities and assortments around customer needs, price positions, and sales channels, working with suppliers and internal teams to bring them into the stores. In some cases, we manufactured the same item under different names for different channels.

I also developed more than 20 category shop-in-shop concepts to organize these broad assortments into understandable destinations. The work connected the product offer with its presentation: what belonged together, how much space it needed, and how teams would merchandise it.
chapters.cap: Products, category concepts and practical store sets.

chapters.text:
The wider Gander program rebuilt and merchandised more than 80 stores in under 18 months, with teams prepared for opening. I ran point on the branding, layout, product, and merchandising work within that shared effort.

As stores opened, a different commercial opportunity became clear. The smaller formats were compact and effective, but filling the larger buildings required more merchandise than the budget could reasonably support. I proposed carving out space for RV sales inside those buildings. The company adopted that approach, putting more of the footprint behind its core business instead of filling every available area with retail inventory.

We then reconsidered smaller underperforming locations. Rather than buying out their leases, we developed the express model: a smaller dealership supported by an extensive logistics system for delivering RVs. My contribution was identifying how the format needed to change and connecting the space, merchandise requirements, and operating model.
chapters.cap: Team rollout and two distinct RV formats.

chapters.text:
This work taught me to keep testing the commercial plan against operating reality. A larger building did not automatically justify a larger assortment, and an underperforming store did not always require a lease exit. Sometimes the better answer was a different use of the space, supported by a different way of serving the customer.

My contribution was connecting those decisions—from products and supplier relationships to layouts, merchandising, and execution with teams. That is the experience I bring to a new business: understanding the opportunity, translating it into practical requirements, and adapting the model when the evidence calls for a change.
chapters.cap: Original annotated RV layout proposal, not an as-built record.

clients.name: Bowery Kitchen Supply
clients.did: I redesigned the store and worked on product records and reporting. The layout and fixtures needed to make a large, varied kitchen assortment easier to shop.

clients.name: W82

clients.name: Denim & Soul

clients.name: American Tea & Coffee

clients.name: The Simple Greek
clients.did: I improved operating routines and developed the retail assortment program across the fast-casual franchise.

rolesData.context: Family office of the Camping World CEO and host of CNBC's The Profit.
rolesData.about: A business development, investment, and operating platform focused on creating, acquiring, and improving businesses across retail, food, manufacturing, and consumer products. Developed new concepts from the first idea through branding, products, packaging, sourcing, and preparation for sale.

chapters.text: I worked across more than 80 operators and companies, from coffee shops and candy stores to pet chains, clothing, restaurants, active sports, and kitchen supply. Each had its own questions to work through. Some were portfolio businesses, others prospective acquisitions, and projects for The Profit also had production deadlines to meet.
chapters.cap: Red Beard Coffee Traders — one of 80+ operators.

chapters.text: I worked inside some businesses and supported others with resources, knowledge, and connections between their operations. I developed more than 15 concepts, covering the business idea, brand, packaging, fixtures, floorplans, sourcing, and products. That included creating American Tea & Coffee and opening its first Texas store. I also worked with The Profit’s production team on builds for upcoming episodes.
chapters.cap: American Tea & Coffee: concept to first store.

chapters.text: Several concepts became physical stores for the show and portfolio companies. At Bentley’s Pet Stuff, I reworked the fixture package from over $100K to under $25K per location, helping make expansion from under 20 to over 100 stores possible. Those practical decisions mattered as much as the look of the stores.
chapters.cap: W82: seven shops-in-shop, one Chicago build.

chapters.text: Working to television deadlines taught me to make an idea clear quickly and then work through what it would take to build it. A storefront drawing was a useful starting point for that conversation. The experience carried into how I approached later projects.
chapters.cap: Making the idea clear enough to move into the build.

rolesData.context: Founder-owned women's fashion boutique chain in high-net-worth Northeast markets.
rolesData.about: A vertically integrated fashion retail and apparel business combining product design, private-label development, international sourcing, merchandising, and multi-unit retail operations. Grew to nine stores in under six months on a high-margin, predominantly private-label assortment, then sold to private equity and continued under ML Fashion Group, which added another eleven locations before the business was folded into a larger group.

chapters.text: My sister and I started COURAGE. b in 2008. We had grown up with our mother in the business, and she had taught us a great deal. We wanted to use that experience to create our own products and keep the margin that came with sourcing them directly. It was a difficult year to start, but we could see an opportunity.
chapters.cap: COURAGE. b — the business my sister and I started in 2008.

chapters.text: The financial crisis made landlords in strong markets more willing to negotiate. We secured discounted leases and opened nine stores in under six months. I ran the business alongside full-time executive roles, working through finance, staffing, merchandising, marketing, production, suppliers, leases, and store development.
chapters.cap: Nine stores in under six months, on crisis-era leases.

chapters.text: We built a production network across France, Italy, China, India, Vietnam, New York, and Los Angeles, matching products to the places best suited to make them. Roughly 90% of the assortment became private label. Developing and sourcing the products gave us much more control over the range and its margin.
chapters.cap: Production across seven locations, sold under one label.

chapters.text: Producing our own range also meant dealing with stock that needed to sell at a discount. We created a separate outlet channel, keeping markdowns out of the core stores. It became the strongest channel by revenue, with net margin close to the full-price stores. The business sold to private equity and continued under ML Fashion Group, which added another eleven locations before it became part of a larger group. The processes and strategy continued to be used after the sale.
chapters.cap: The outlet channel — markdown revenue that protected core margin.

rolesData.context: Iconic multi-channel specialty retailer — roughly 150 stores plus catalog and web.
rolesData.about: An iconic American consumer-products brand known for bringing innovative electronics, gadgets, and lifestyle merchandise to the mass market through specialty stores, catalogs, and direct marketing. At its peak it operated nearly 200 stores at the intersection of technology, product innovation, gifting, and lifestyle retail.

chapters.text: I joined as Manager for Trend Analysis, a role I thought of as Director of Cool. The board wanted to bring fresh products and a sense of discovery back to a 150-store chain. Finding things customers had not seen before was a brief I could get excited about.
chapters.cap: The Sharper Image floor — a brand built on surprise.

chapters.text: I looked through supplier contacts and blogs for new products, then moved into the Director of Product Development role. The work expanded into product development, store displays, and how products appeared across stores, the catalog, and the website. I worked directly with the CEO on the direction of the business and merchandising priorities.
chapters.cap: New products, built from trend signal to shelf.

chapters.text: I negotiated co-op funding and developed plans across the website, catalog, and stores that generated approximately $1M annually. I also helped develop the licensing business, which continued beyond the stores.
chapters.cap: Connecting the catalog with stores and the website.

chapters.text: That experience connected product discovery with how a customer encounters a brand. A product had to make sense on a shelf, on a catalog page, and online. The licensing work added another way for the brand and its products to reach people.
chapters.cap: Licensing gave the brand another route to customers.

rolesData.context: New York advertising agency; new-business development group.
rolesData.about: Kirshenbaum Bond + Partners — a New York agency founded in 1987 that grew into one of the largest independent advertising firms in the U.S., known for disruptive creative, guerrilla marketing, and media innovation for brands including BMW, Target, Citi, Tommy Hilfiger, and Delta Air Lines.

chapters.text: I joined the new-business development group, working with senior executives to win clients and develop work for existing accounts. I was the point person on a group of accounts we won, starting with Priceline.com. I helped build the pitch by working through the positioning, the competition, and how to explain the opportunity. Online travel was still proving it could retain customers without a storefront. Priceline’s “name your own price” proposition needed to feel like a smart choice rather than a gamble; the pitch had to make that clear.
chapters.cap: Priceline.com — the pitch that opened the run.

chapters.text: Mrs. Butterworth’s brought a different kind of question. It was already a recognizable brand, so the pitch had to show how it could stay relevant alongside private label and lower-priced alternatives. I worked on connecting the creative thinking with the retail questions: what sells, what earns margin, and what deserves shelf space. Recognition alone would not protect its place on the shelf. Grocery buyers needed a case built around sales velocity and margin per facing, as well as a strong creative idea.
chapters.cap: Mrs. Butterworth's — the first major consumer products win.

chapters.text: The wins also included Diageo, Edward Jones, and Snapple. Moving between travel, consumer products, financial services, and spirits meant getting to understand a different business each time. That variety was a big part of what I enjoyed about the work. For Diageo, the question was how a challenger agency could handle a portfolio of brands competing for attention in a crowded spirits market. The idea had to distinguish the brands, rather than depend only on spending more on advertising.
chapters.cap: Diageo — one of the new-business accounts we won.

chapters.text: The Sharper Image became both a client and my next employer. Working on the account took me into the products, stores, catalog, and website, and the business later hired me directly. It was the move from helping explain what a retailer could do to taking responsibility for putting it into practice.
chapters.cap: The Sharper Image — the client that became the next job.

items.name: Retail Operations
items.story: Over the past 30+ years, I have dedicated my career to refining retail operations by creating seamless, customer-focused environments that drive profitability. My hands-on methodology bridges high-level executive strategy with the realities of day-to-day store execution. I believe that true operational excellence stems from empowering frontline teams and establishing clear, scalable processes that everyone can understand. aiProjectsData.label: Real-Time Audio · Adaptive Audio Engine · Hardware Link · AI-Assisted Build
bullets: Started as a real DJ app running in the browser — four decks, real audio, MIDI hardware support, track analysis, and saved libraries — and grew into ATOMIQ LIVE 1.0, a complete performance system.

The Adaptive Audio Engine is the system's shared clock: decks, waveforms, stems, hardware lights, and visuals all stay in time with the music's phrase, key, and energy. The software spots the moment; the DJ makes the call.

Tested like serious software: hardware control passed 400/400 checks three runs in a row, the interface 489/489, and the intelligence layer 433/433 — with mix scoring proven against a 5,000-track library.

The intelligence picks the best next track, explains exactly how to mix into it, and can even mix on its own — but the moment the DJ touches a fader, control snaps back instantly. It helps the performer, never replaces them.

The product site, the live browser booth (desktop and phone), hardware connections, video output for the crowd, and one unified music library were all built with AI as the tools (Grok + Claude) — directed like a product team, not generated as a mockup.

aiMinisData.text: An AI-operated e-commerce model: six specialist agents own research, design, content, listings, scheduling, and analysis while the human retains approval and strategic control. The early expression of the agent thesis PARKOUR later formalized.

aiFlowData.name: Define the business problem
aiFlowData.desc: Talk through where time is lost, what people need, and what would make the work easier.

aiFlowData.name: Research what already exists
aiFlowData.desc: Look at existing tools, previous work, and the constraints before deciding what needs to be built.
aiFlowData.output: A reuse, connect, or build decision

aiFlowData.name: Agree what the tool must do
aiFlowData.desc: Write down the users, the steps, the screens, and what a useful result looks like.

aiFlowData.name: Map the system
aiFlowData.desc: Work through how information moves, which tools connect, and where people make decisions.

aiFlowData.name: Give each AI a clear job
aiFlowData.desc: Use separate agents for defined tasks, with shared instructions and clear handoffs.
aiFlowData.output: Work that can move in parallel

aiFlowData.name: Keep the work in one place
aiFlowData.desc: Save the code, decisions, and handoffs in GitHub so the next person can follow what happened.

aiFlowData.name: Build and connect in small pieces
aiFlowData.desc: Put one useful part in place, check it, and connect it to the next.

aiFlowData.name: Test the actual work
aiFlowData.desc: Check the numbers, the steps, and what happens when something goes wrong.

aiFlowData.name: Review before release
aiFlowData.desc: I review the important decisions and the result before it goes into use.

aiFlowData.name: Use it and improve it
aiFlowData.desc: Learn from the people using it, remove friction, and carry that learning into the next version.

aiStoryData.title: It starts with a working session
aiStoryData.lead: Every build opens as a conversation about a real business problem. One AI shapes the architecture and product direction; another pressure-tests the reasoning before anything is committed.

aiStoryData.title: The research goes wide
aiStoryData.lead: Independent agents scan the market, the competition, and the evidence from different angles — so no single model's blind spots decide anything.

aiStoryData.title: Design becomes working prototypes
aiStoryData.lead: Interfaces are designed as real, clickable prototypes — not static mockups — then packaged into clear communication for stakeholders.

aiStoryData.title: Several builders work at once
aiStoryData.lead: Implementation runs in parallel: multiple coding agents build separate parts of the system in their own lanes, under one set of standards.

aiStoryData.title: Everything lands in one place
aiStoryData.lead: GitHub is the durable source of truth. Every branch, decision record, handoff, and automated check lives in the repository — nothing important stays in a chat window.

tools.name: GitHub
tools.role: Durable source of truth · Branches · Handoffs

aiStoryData.title: Images and video, produced in-house
aiStoryData.lead: Visual assets are generated, upscaled, and finished at production quality without leaving the workflow.

aiStoryData.title: The business runs on live data
aiStoryData.lead: Operational data stays in systems the whole team — human and AI — can read and write: sheets, shared files, and executive dashboards.
